utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there were two short preliminary matters to be raised by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and good morning, Your Honours. First, one leftover matter from yesterday. We'd discussed towards the end of the day 65 ter 08036. There had been a question on the transcript about whether it was -- that Mr. Lukic had raised about whether it was the same document discussed in a portion of the witness's previous testimony that I showed him. We've looked together at that testimony a little bit more thoroughly. We agree, first, that it was the same document; and second, that it should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And no number was yet reserved for it. Therefore, Madam Registrar, for 65 ter 08036, what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P07103, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7103 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the second, very briefly, Your Honour, and I don't think it will take longer than it would take the witness to be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness already be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is simply to say that I'm aware that the witness has been advised of his rights under Rule 90(E) in previous cases, and I think the questions I ask him or anticipate asking him this morning may raise some of the issues that prompted that advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you know that the Chamber is guided by the parties who know what questions will be put to the witness, and I'll follow your suggestion to inform the witness about his rights under Rule 90(E). Meanwhile, I also use the time, and I'm addressing the Defence, Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was recently informed by the Victims and Witness Section that the average stay in The Hague for Defence witnesses has increased over the last few months. The Chamber is aware that it can be difficult to arrange for witnesses to be available without interruption. At the same time, this difficulty should not lead to having witnesses stay in The Hague for close to two weeks, and the Defence is instructed to pay closer attention to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's anything to be said, Mr. Lukic, then perhaps we hear from you after we have concluded the -- hearing the evidence of Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pasic. Three Judges again today. Mr. Pasic, before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. That's one. And, second, having reviewed the transcript and video of yesterday's hearing, I'd like to urge you to answer questions directly and not to stay away from what the question is. Mr. Traldi will now continue his -- yes, no, before we continue, I have to -- the -- I was asked to inform you about Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal. And I'll read it to you: "A witness," that's, in this case, it's you, "may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." I think yesterday you were -- it was mentioned that you are a trained lawyer, and therefore, may I take it that you understand this rule and that you'll not hesitate to, if you are afraid that a truthful answer might incriminate you, to address me if you would rather not answer that question because you are under no obligation to answer questions which would incriminate you -- if the answers would incriminate you. Mr. Traldi, you may proceed. And I do understand there's another half-hour to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We provided clean statement for this gentleman since he really had a problem with reading from the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- then it can be provided to him. Meanwhile, Mr. Traldi, you may already start.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, to start, I noticed we had a small difference in terminology yesterday. Do you know -- or do you agree with me, yes or no, that your municipality was known as Bosanski Novi before the war and was renamed Novi Grad after the Muslims had left?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in 1992 its name was changed to Novi Grad. Actually, it happened to be the old name of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so when I refer to Bosanski Novi and you refer to Novi Grad, we're talking about the same municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now we were talking yesterday about the Japra valley. And because there was a war on, all of the Muslim citizens of the Japra valley were disarmed; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a number of operations involving disarming. It is difficult to say, though, whether everyone was disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's look at very briefly 65 ter 31937, page 97; this will be another portion of your OTP interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down just slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you were asked first: "My question was and you -- you -- you're free to talk, but my question was why this particular group of people, the citizens of the Japra valley, been completely disarmed, because if ... because they were Muslims, right?" And you said: "They were disarmed because it was a war." And you explained in your next answer that in your view Bosanski Novi couldn't exist as an oasis. And then you were asked: "All right. So because there was a war on, all of the Muslim citizens of this area, Japra valley, were disarmed?" And you answered: "Of course." So do you stand by the truthfulness and accuracy of the answer you gave in 2003?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do. I didn't say anything otherwise. I wanted to say that it is difficult to say that whether 100 per cent of them were disarmed. There was always this possibility that someone hid their weapons. It was an option. It actually proved to be true, because some people could later on still be found with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We saw yesterday you said that you couldn't guarantee the Muslims' safety in that area, and it was because of actions like those taken by the Territorial Defence and the police that we looked at yesterday, the shelling of these Muslim village, the crimes committed by the special unit of the Banja Luka CSB, that you were not in a position to guarantee these Muslims safety; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not so. The special unit, if we mentioned it yesterday, we mentioned it regarding Kostajnica. It's a different area. There were some incidents there and we asked that the special police be withdrawn to Banja Luka. In the Japra valley there was no special police, at least to my knowledge, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So let me ask the question very simply: It was because of crimes being committed at -- by the TO and by the police that you couldn't guarantee the Muslims safety in the Japra valley. Do you agree, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. Security could not be guaranteed to due to the presence of paramilitary formations, small groups and individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have page 91 of the same interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you're discussing here Muslims from the Japra valley coming to the Bosanski Novi Municipal Assembly, and you're asked what you did in those negotiations. And you answered: "This is exactly what the Muslim representatives were asking to leave the area because they didn't feel safe and secure. Because they were asking, because they were asking us, the municipal authorities, they were asking us to guarantee them full security and safety, whether we could do that. And unfortunately we told them the truth, which was the truth, that we were in no position with this formation of the SJB unit and the TO Staff, that we were not in a position to guarantee them full safety and security." Now, what you were saying was it was because of the police and the TO that you, the Crisis Staff, didn't feel in a position to guarantee them safety and security; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We could not guarantee their safety for the simple reason that it was impossible to engage sufficient numbers of people that could -- who could guard every Muslim house and defend it. That is why we did not guarantee their safety. It's not a matter of the police or the TO. They were not the ones committing crimes. Let me repeat: There were some paramilitary formations that were very difficult to suppress and monitor. That was the problem. The police was not the problem. The TO was not the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, I have a couple of follow-up questions. First, we looked at the Crisis Staff report yesterday. We saw that members of TO units had been the ones shelling these villages in the Japra valley and expelling Muslims, according to the report of your Crisis Staff. So, clearly, the TO wouldn't have been who you would have call on to protect the Muslims under those circumstances, knowing that. So I'd put to you that what you were talking about here, what you were saying here, was that you were concerned, and the SJB unit and the TO, your inability to stop them from committing crimes against the Muslims, was what you meant here. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would object here. I think that it misrepresents the evidence and we can watch -- look at the document, and I will point to the exact portion of this document. In B/C/S version, it's page 3, penultimate paragraph; and in English, it's page 5, paragraph 2, when it is talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before you do so, I noticed that if -- what you could do is you could invite Mr. Traldi to specifically refer to specific portions in his question, and if there's any other matter still to be considered, you can do that in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, when I referred to crimes by the TO appearing in your report on the work of the Crisis Staff, what I specifically was referring to was the language in that report saying members of the TO units in Agic, Rujinka, and Krsalj, had conducted armed activities which included the use of mortars and caused the expulsion of Muslim civilians from a number of villages. And what I'd put to you was that under those circumstances, knowing that at the time, the only plausible explanation of what you were saying here was that the TO in its expulsion of these Muslims was part of why you didn't think you could guarantee their safety. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a very long question and not easy to answer. There is a string of questions, actually. Let me repeat: First of all, the TO was not involved in the commission of crimes in the way you present it. There were no such operations. You simply perhaps do not wish to understand that on the other side too there were formations that would then change into civilian clothes. There were Muslim paramilitary formations being active --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. He cannot be stopped now. He is explaining exactly why he does not agree with Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you close -- we close his mouth, he cannot explain the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think the witness moves away, and it's not for the first time, from what he was asked, whether there were opposing parties. What Mr. Traldi did is he put a specific portion of a report. He was not talking about crimes anymore but he was talking about operations. To that extent, he has more or less adapted the language in view of apparently what you objected to. And now the question is what the witness meant, whether it's the only reasonable explanation of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I hesitate to intervene at this moment, but just to clarify: The part I'd put was that these operations caused the expulsion of those civilians, and so I don't think that we would agree that that's not criminal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that's argument, or rather debate. I stick strictly to what you read to the witness. And apparently the witness says that this is not the only reasonable explanation of his words. Witness, you explained to us earlier that it was the SJB and TO shortage of persons that you referred to here. That is what you wanted to further explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. We had a problem during that period with the size of those formations of the TO and the civilian police. They were simply not there in sufficient numbers to be able to guarantee safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when Mr. Traldi again insisted on his interpretation of your words, you say you still disagree. It's still your old explanation. Let's move on, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to turn now to the train taking the Muslims from Blagaj out of Bosanski Novi that we left off with yesterday. I'm going to ask whether you agree with a couple of simple propositions to start. First, do you agree that after the train departed Novi it was stopped, the men were taken off, and several hundred of them were returned to Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were moving in the direction of Banja Luka, Doboj, and Zenica. They were supposed to leave the area of Doboj and move further to Zenica which was under Muslim forces' control. That is how they were supposed to go to the other side. A certain number of people in Doboj, whom I don't know, took a part of that population - that is to say, able-bodied men - and returned them to Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And those men were detained in the Mlakve stadium after they were returned to Bosanski Novi; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were held in the stadium at Mlakve for safety reasons. It was the assessment at the time that should they return and they were able bodied, there were some fears on the part of the Serbs in terms of whether we would be again able to protect our population if they returned to the area of Japra.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they had lent armed resistance before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: None of them were armed at this point obviously; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there were concerns that they still had hidden weapons in their villages that they left behind. That was the reason for the assessment. It was for the reason -- for reasons of their safety and the safety of the rest of the population, the Serb population, so that they would not cause additional incidents having caused them previously, such as armed clashes. So, simply put: They were not to be trusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And they were detained in the stadium until the 22nd or 23rd of July, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have to say I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people left --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- others came within a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. He was exactly answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Once the witness says "I don't know," I think I'm well within my rights to call up his previous statement on the subject for efficiency if nothing else, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness says he doesn't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But he explained what happened, why he does not know exactly how long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But the question was not why do you not know, the question was what happened. And if the witness says, "I don't know," then you -- in re-examination, you can further explore the reasons why he may not have had any knowledge which you -- where the reasons are considered by the Defence to be relevant. We move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was audio record of what the witness said. We asked for that to be entered into the transcript. What he said. He answered further than it was recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- that's a totally different matter. Whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I'm raising a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, these are two different matters. You objected to the question, that's first of all, and if there's anything lost which was not translated, then you know how we proceed; that is, we'll have it verified on the basis of the audio and we'll take care that our record will be complete. Apparently you heard what he said. You can make any request to have the transcript be completed. And since you know what he said, you can still address the matter in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I'm afraid that it could cause confusion on the part of the witness since he already said that and nobody knows what he said. I would rather have it -- him repeat how he finished his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- let's perhaps, in order to avoid confusion, Witness, apparently your last words were not put on the record. Could you repeat them? After you said that you didn't know whether they were detained until, what was it, I think in the 22nd or 23rd of July. You said you don't know. And what did you then add? No new answers. Just to repeat what you said then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe that some people left and others came to the reception centre at Mlakve. I cannot say with any certainty whether all those people remained until the date specified by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: One reason you can't say with certainty is you were never at the stadium yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I wasn't involved in such operative work later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, during that period, however, you were negotiating with representatives of the international community about the movement of Muslims from Bosanski Novi. During those negotiations, they warned you that it was against international humanitarian law to forcibly displace people from their homes based on ethnic reasons, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had several conversations to that effect, and such issues were raised during those meetings. Given the fact that you keep interrupting me, I cannot elaborate it any further, because you wouldn't let me talk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the question that matter was addressed. Please proceed. If Mr. Traldi wants further details, then he'll ask for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And they expressed reluctance to assist with the Muslims leaving because they didn't want to be part of what they considered to be ethnic cleansing; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. They were not reluctant. They talked for days and then they agreed when they realised that they did want to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's look at two of the statements by one of the negotiators you mention in your statement, Jean-Claude Concolato, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter 11607. 11607.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is an article published by Reuters on the 27th of July 1992. In the third paragraph, we read: "More than 10.000 Muslims from Bosanski Novi in Bosnia were evacuated to Croatia by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees last week, telling of killings and terror at the hands of Serb militias." Now, that's the evacuation that you were referring to that the United Nations eventually agreed to assist with; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This text does say who did what and what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So, yes, that's the evacuation you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I assume. I don't know what Reuters wrote. The UN evacuating the Muslim population. That is what is referred to, is it? UNPROFOR that existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what Mr. Concolato says about why they assisted is not that they were convinced that the Muslims wanted to leave. He says at the end of the fourth paragraph: "They were blackmailed by Serb militiamen into evacuating them." And in the fifth paragraph, it quotes his words explaining: "The blackmail was very simple, he said. It consisted of saying to us that if you don't evacuate these people, bad things will happen. While we were there, bad things did happen - two explosions and a Muslim was killed by sniper." Now, that's the message you and other Serb leaders delivered to the UN representatives: If you don't evacuate them, bad things will happen; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. You did not read that somebody from the paramilitaries threatened Jean-Claude Concolato. I never belonged to any paramilitary formations, and you compared me to them now, and that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let's look at another of his statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to understand your testimony fully, are you saying that what is reported here was said during conversations with paramilitaries and not with any of the -- any of your people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation I received was that Jean-Claude Concolato was blackmailed by the paramilitaries, not by me or any of the official municipal organs. At least that's the interpretation that I received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's not what you read, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm not sure how the word "militiamen" would have been translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Militiamen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- Your Honour. But I think to be of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let me just ... let me just -- I'm trying to find where you used the expression "militiamen."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Yes, that was one of the previous paragraphs. Now, this conversation where it was said that bad things would happen if they would not evacuate, was that part of your conversation you had with -- with the UNHCR representatives, the UN representatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We talked to the UNHCR and I certainly cannot give you an exact quote as to what was said, but we did explain to them the reasons, the needs, that existed in Novi Grad, and that we were explaining the safety of the population there. That was the conversation. However, I cannot quote it unambiguously now. That I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the gist of it, that if they wouldn't leave that you couldn't guarantee their safety and that bad things would happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I repeat, I cannot say whether that's exactly the way we had put it. But unfortunately in a war only bad things happen. That is logical. That such variance had to be taken into account, that some unpleasant things could happen. And I repeat, certain paramilitary formations that were not under the command of the municipal authorities or the military authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everyone accepts that bad things can happen during a war. That is when you evacuate and also when you do not evacuate. War is war. That's fully understood by everyone in this courtroom. Did you make any link between bad things would happen if they would not evacuate? If you don't remember, tell us, but that's the simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we always chose the lesser evil, and in that way we wanted to meet the needs of the population so that they would feel safer wherever it was that they were. That was the aim of these conversations and talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you urge them to leave in order to avoid the lesser evil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we did not encourage them or urge them to go. And I keep saying that. What is being said all the time is that we expelled them. The point was that they themselves decided to leave, and there were several motives why they asked to leave the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if at the very end they decide that they want to leave, that doesn't necessarily mean that they were not urged to leave being warned about bad things that could happen to them. If you don't see that, we'll have to move on. But if you agree with that, then ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not quite understand that question. Could you kindly repeat it, please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You emphasise again and again that they decided to leave. Now, that is still possible if you're urged to leave because bad things may happen to you, you may finally decide that you hardly have any choice and that the only thing you can do is to leave. So the one doesn't exclude the other. That's what I'm putting to you, and I'm asking you whether you agree with that or not, irrespective of what may have happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look, we did not make these assessments by ourselves. When I say "we" I'm talking about the Serb organs. There were some Muslim representatives that were involved too, and all this is supported by previous statements that were given, including Muslims who said that they wanted to leave. So I believe that there is no contest there. At first they even said that that was their plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed that you stick to emphasise the decision-making by the Muslims and more or less avoiding what may have happened before and the possibilities of that. Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just going to point you to one thing in this document. This is Mr. Concolato giving a statement in the press again. You said the UN wasn't reluctant to assist because they considered it ethnic cleansing. They were happy to do it because the Bosnians wanted to leave. In the third paragraph, Mr. Concolato is quoted from an interview with the Associated Press and he says: "We have been forced to take part in this monstrous policy of ethnic cleansing." And then he describes in the next paragraph the convoy of Muslims out of Bosanski Novi on the 23rd of July. In fact, the United Nations publicly stated that they considered what was happening there to be ethnic cleansing. That's the truth, isn't it? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they stated, I don't know, and I cannot give you just a yes or no answer. Now whether they committed the crime of ethnic cleansing, that is for you to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 11607 and 31968.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 11607 receives number P7104. And document 31968 receives number P7105, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7104 and P7105 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one more topic. It -- starting it will require us briefly to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is the testimony of a witness in the Krajisnik case named Emin Puric, and he's asked by the Presiding Judge in that case if the issue of the Muslims in Bosanski Novi returning to the places they lived was ever discussed during the negotiations with you. He replies, beginning at line 19: "No, it was pointless to even mention this to them. It was a question that had no sense at all at that point. We wanted to leave, to save our lives ..." When you say the Muslims in Bosanski Novi wanted to leave, when you say they left voluntarily, what you mean is they wanted to leave to save their lives. That's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you've just read out the statement of Mr. Puric who said in that statement, if it was interpreted properly, yet again, and I did not want to offend anyone, I repeat that yet again, he stated that they wanted to leave and I believe that this statement is contradictory in relation to the previous questions that we discussed. Nobody knew how long the war would go on. Nobody knew whether the safety and security situation would be all right. It was a time of war, chaos, killings, et cetera, when indeed people did not know that safety in the territory of Novi Grad or in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina would be restored. It was impossible to establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Lukic, we have five minutes until the break. We could also take an earlier break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would prefer to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have a break now. Could you give us an indication as to how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I noticed Mr. Traldi that after introducing document P7103, that I will have then to have lengthy re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And just to put clearly on the record, I'd used one specific part of the document during cross-examination and would expect that re-direct related to that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. It will not relate only to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see to what extent the questions in re-examination are related to what was asked during cross-examination. There are certain limits --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, but I can vouch that it will relate only to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, I'm not ruling. Not knowing what your questions will be, Mr. Lukic, it's useless for us to further discuss that. We'll wait and see what happens. Mr. Pasic, you're invited to follow the usher. We'll take a break and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could address one brief matter in private session before we break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll briefly turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you'll now be re-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are nearing the end. My learned friend Mr. Traldi asked you about paragraph 43 of your statement. You can go to it, or yet it's necessary. I will just tell you it involves the destruction of a mosque. In the paragraph itself you said that it was not an organised way that mosques were destroyed in, and in a sentence after that you say the government had a lot of problems with paramilitary formations. These paramilitary formations appear later on in your statement as well. In order to fully appreciate your testimony, please tell us where those paramilitary formations came from to the area of Novi Grad municipality or Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Thank you for protecting me previously. The paramilitary formations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you refrain from such statements. Mr. Lukic puts questions to you, and Mr. Lukic now and then objects to what the Prosecution does, just as the Prosecution objects sometimes to what the Defence does. It's not for you - and I repeat that now - to make implicit comments on who is doing his job well or not well and why they are doing it. Would you please keep that in mind? And, again, you are at risk to invalidate your own testimony, and that's certainly not what you want, I take it. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic. Perhaps we invite the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, please tell us where the paramilitary formations came from.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When discussing the topic of paramilitary formations and some small groups and individuals. Unfortunately, those formations for the most part came from the area of the then-Krajina, which is now in Croatia. The war had begun there a year before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. People became armed and there was a proportion of the people who illegally obtained weapons. Their only motive was material gain. They had criminal motives and they began creating problems. I have to say that we had a lot of such paramilitary formations causing problems. Oftentimes they didn't choose their means and didn't care whose property it was. Their only goal was to get to some booty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to show you P7099 - it has already been shown to you - from the municipal TO Staff. It requested additional ammunition and weapons on the 16th of March, 1992. At the time in mid-March 1992, were the staff of the TO and the TO itself under the command of the Sarajevo TO Staff or were they outside of the system of the TO Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was outside of the system. It was still at the time of much turbulence. At the time, the JNA was still formally in existence and the TO was supposed to be a part of it. In that period of time, I think, there was still the single TO Staff in operation. I apologise. At the time, there was still Muslim personnel in the TO Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us look at P7100 briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the document you were unable to read. It is the document of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Novi municipality dated the 8th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at another document in relation to this one. It is P7101. It is a document of the Bosanski Novi municipality Red Cross of the previous day, which is to say the 7th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph reads: "For several weeks now, the Serbian army has been involved in war operations against Muslim extremists in the Bosanski Novi area." Do you recall any wartime operations in the area of your municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It was the worst period in May and June. That is when these war operations took place. For some operational reasons, these paramilitary groups would often change into civilian clothes; hence, the confusion and belief that we were going after civilians. It wasn't true. These people would change between their military uniform and civilian clothes to mutate, so to speak, thus causing confusion and coming from the rear, endangering safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next sentence reads: "The result of these operations is a large concentration of Muslim people in Blagaj. Their accommodation in Blagaj is temporary because representatives of the displaced Muslims have asked for voluntary resettlement in Croatia." Let me ask you this: How did it happen that the Muslims became so concentrated in the area of Blagaj, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, they believed that a smaller area, such as the village of Blagaj, was safer for them. They believed that there would be no incidents or uncomfortable situations. In the meantime, there had already been attempts with the high commissioner for refugees in Dvor Una and Topusko. So they were already participating in it. I won't go into their reasons again, but they wished to go towards Croatia and further on to Europe. It was their plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We should go into the private session, Your Honours, for a second to protect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, in the third paragraph of this document that is before us -- you don't have to read it. I know that you have trouble reading from the screen. It says: "Also, operations are under way to cleanse the area around Blagaj of Muslim extremists who are hiding in the surrounding woods. Due to these operations, there is a real danger of some groups getting out of the command and control ... and threatening the safety of people in Blagaj." At Crisis Staff meetings, did you discuss military operations taking place in and around Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the rule was that usually the chief of police, who was on the Crisis Staff, and the TO Staff commander would briefly inform us about the situation on the ground because they were the operatives who had the most adequate information from the field. And, of course, they did inform us about things like that, that were a threat from this or that side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I put a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you read this document, you're not the author, could you tell us how you understand the reference to certain -- "some groups getting out of the command and the control mechanism." What groups? Are you thinking of in terms of Bosnians, are you thinking in terms of Serbs? When you read this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I stated yesterday that at one point in time -- I don't know exactly what the time reference would be. But at one point in time, some people from the regional staff did not act in accordance with the instructions of the TO Staff and measures were taken, so this did happen from the Serb side but there were also these Muslim groups that did not want to surrender their weapons, that is to say, they put up a resistance, and of course this created tension and fear among the rest of the population; that is to say, on both sides there were such problems, both on the Serb and Muslim sides. So some people had already surrendered weapons and were not putting up a resistance, but part of the Muslim population that even wore civilian uniforms or rather civilian clothing did put up this resistance in these woods, thickets, forests, hills around their own houses or neighbours' houses and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let's keep matters simple. So apparently you understand "groups" here to refer to Muslim groups, not Serbs. Here, in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, well, I'd have to read the entire text in order to see what the author was trying to say. But my assumption is that there were problems on both sides in my view. Actually, this is my conclusion. I mean, as I've said, I would need to read the entire text in order to understand the meaning that the author of the text had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us look at P7103 now, please. This is a report of the -- on the work of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've seen this document. Your name is at the end, it hasn't been signed, but now it is in evidence, and I'm going to ask you something about what you knew at the time. In line 13 in this text from the top, in the English version it is line 10, this is what it says: "It was requested that the TO units in the field be linked up and systemised in terms of formation, that a command be established," and so on and so forth. Do you know which period is being referred to here and whether the situation was like this in the TO, whether things were disorganised?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's the very beginning. Perhaps one could say May, June probably, and that speaks of the technical capacities of the TO Staff; namely, they were not properly equipped -- I don't know. This was information, if I understood it correctly. I don't know whether this document was sent further up to higher-ranking organs to improve the technical situation because often in the field one felt that the communication system was not functioning adequately and, of course, at the time there weren't such technical things like mobile telephones and so on and so forth. So this was the request made to make this kind of improvement, so there would be synchronisation among units so that these kind of unpleasant things would not happen. If we would informed on time, then we could take action in order to put a stop to any problem in the field. I mean, that is the point of this kind of report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us take a look at the next paragraph, further down, line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2 in English; again, line 4 from the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is what this report says: "Would it be possible through negotiations to defuse the danger of war and find a peaceful solution to the crisis?" And then further down, please, line 6 from the bottom. In English, it is the fifth line from the bottom of the page. It says: "One has to speak to representatives of the SDA all the time and find a peaceful solution." Which period is this, Mr. Pasic? And, in practice, did this happen?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is confirmed by my entire testimony. We thought all the time that these were official political representatives at that time. At that moment, the SDA was the party that Muslims belonged to, and we believed that they were legitimate representatives and that they could legitimately in a way influence the rest of the Muslim population. I think that this is precisely the period that I mentioned; that is to say, before and after these unfortunate conflicts, May, June, even part of July, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic. Now let us look at the last sentence on this page, and it is page 2 in English, the very last sentence in paragraph 1. It says: "The Crisis Staff pointed out that all armed individuals outside the TO are paramilitaries and that they must either be placed under control or disarmed." Do you remember who you meant here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to object on several grounds. First, I think this has been leading and leading on portions of a document that didn't come up during cross-examination. Second, the disarmament order that comes up in the witness's statement and he wasn't crossed about that, but it's clearly discussed in the statement and wasn't cross-examined about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic how --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document is allegedly composed by this gentleman. I don't know whom else should we discussed with the documents that are in the evidence introduced by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If -- Your Honours, the Defence was clearly on notice from the witness's previous testimonies that he was able to comment on this document. If the Defence chooses not to use their court time in direct examination on a document, going through it in detail in re-direct because one portion of it has been used on cross-examination, I would submit, is neither an efficient nor a proper use of the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there seems to be a dispute about whether your right to re-examine the witness is focusing on the subject matter of cross-examination or whether it's just a formal link with a document which was used, although not in those respects. Let me just confer with my colleagues for one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may say something, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it's undisputed between us and the Prosecution that there was intention on Mr. Pasic's side of the Crisis Staff of Novi Grad at that time to disarm everybody who was illegally armed, we would not have -- it wouldn't be necessary for us to pose this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course that matter is disputed. The point is that to ask that question by pointing to a document the Defence is on notice of for the first time on redirect examination is simply not, in my submission, proper. It's increasingly improper to do it when similar assertions are in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We received this document when the cross started from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is document, aside from being discussed in both of the witness's previous testimonies, has been on our 65 ter list, so the Defence has had access to it since at least February of 2012. To say they received the document for the first time yesterday is misleading --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Let me stop you there at this moment. I don't think that the claim by Mr. Lukic is that he had no access to this document. It's just that he says that it really would be used. And of course, we often find long lists. A 65 ter list is pretty long. Then the lists which are provided for documents to be used in cross-examination indeed are relatively long as well and are received only briefly before. But let me, as I announced earlier, briefly confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties have to be selective some way in what they can deal with in the limited time provided. The Chamber has tried to analyse the situation. Mr. Traldi, do you want the Chamber to rely on any other portion of this document you did not deal with in cross-examination? And are you, for example, willing to limit even or to -- to make a selection of matters you consider it to be important? Because if you are not, then of course all of it is in evidence, and then Mr. Lukic should have an opportunity to ask further questions about it. But if you limit yourself to the portions you dealt with, then we might decide otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In this case, Your Honour, we would rely on the document, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Lukic has an opportunity to put further questions to the witness about the content of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I warned Mr. Traldi if he is going to introduce this document that I will have to have lengthy re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you brought to his attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, not warned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Lukic has developed this very unfortunate practice of threatening me lately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I know that you're a strong man, Mr. Traldi, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have that -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As long as Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... really threatened by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As long as Mr. Lukic is not an overlapping speaker and still laughs, which does not appear on the transcript, then we take it that we might move in the right direction. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Pasic, what was the intention that you had at the Crisis Staff? Do you remember that there were discussions about this, that all armed persons who were outside the TO should either placed under control or disarmed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely what the thinking was, and that can be supported by a great many other things; namely, that we insisted that all these paramilitary formations should be neutralised. They should be disarmed or perhaps part of these people should be mobilised in military terms and become part of the TO or the civilian police. Irrespective of ethnic background, that's what we insisted upon. I don't know whether you're going to ask me about this, but I would just like to present this argument; namely, that we had a great problem with part of these small groups. And there was even a killing that occurred, a Serb was killed. I think that that was documented during my previous testimony when a man who belonged to a paramilitary formation and who resisted the law had to be liquidate physically by the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The person who was killed is of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me correctly, I think it was Miroslav Petic. He belonged to, how do I put this, a criminal group that operated there. They also called them Suva Rebra, dry ribs, and unfortunately he had to be liquidated because he resisted the civilian police and they had no other choice. But he is an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are moving chronologically now we are dealing with the 20th of April. It says here that on the 20th of April part of the Novi Battalion that was stationed in Jasenovac came to Bosanski Novi and raised a Serb flag there using the threat of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 2 in B/C/S. Page 2 in English, the third paragraph, that's where that is all stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says this was assessed to be a certain incident and the Crisis Staff could not agree to that. What was your reactions? Do you remember, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do remember that moment. I don't know the exact date, but I think it was precisely on that date the Crisis Staff thought that this kind of forceful raising of the flag could be disproved of by the other part of the population, the Muslim population, and our assessment was that in this way people could be irritated in a way, and we simply thought that that was not the right move. That was the thinking of the Crisis Staff. That is to say, our view was that that should not have been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3 in B/C/S now, page 4 in English. In the B/C/S version, we need paragraph 3 from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will see that it starts with the words: "While implementing ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the English version, we need the paragraph -- page 4, paragraph 2 from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this is what it says: "Regarding the implementation of the government decision on disarming in the time-period from the 5th to the 11th of May, the Crisis Staff representatives invested a lot of effort in negotiations with the SDA representatives in order to implement the disarming action peacefully." These negotiations for the SDA, could you tell us who took part in that, just briefly, and what kind of agreement was reached, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not going to say 100 per cent, but for the most part I took part in this and other members of the Crisis Staff; those who were involved in particular topics, if I can put it that way. Our aim was to prevent a conflict, to establish some kind of peace although there was a war waging around us already, and we made all conceivable efforts to try to prevent a conflict in Novi Grad. That was the aim of all of these talks and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who took part in these talks from the SDA side?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was Izet Mehmedagic, their president, in say 90 per cent of all cases. Some people would also come along. I mean, their hierarchy was a bit stronger. They respect the fact that somebody is their president. Unfortunately, the Serbs don't really feel that way. So he attended all of these meetings. I have to admit, and I have to say, unfortunately this man lost his life after that. At that moment, he did show, I don't know what his inner thoughts were, but he did show that he wanted to have peace. And very often he said that at these talks. If there is a conflict -- now, I mean, was he aware of the situation that the Muslims were in? He said that their plan was to leave the territory of the municipality of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next paragraph which is the last in the English version and the following in the B/C/S reads: "On the 11th of May after the deadline for the surrender of weapons had passed and after the incident involving military police patrol in Blagaj, armed conflict started on town territory." What was this incident involving the military police a patrol, what is it about?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened on the main road between Novi Grad and Prijedor, some 6 to 7 kilometres away from Novi Grad. It was sometime in the evening hours, as far as I know between 10.00 and 12.00 in the evening. In that Muslim location of Blagaj, some unknown perpetrators - unknown to us, that is - opened fire at the police patrol from the TO Staff. There were no victims but one person was lightly wounded. Of course, the vehicle was also damaged. It was the first armed incident that took place. Unfortunately, it proved to be fatal because that is when all those difficult operations and days ensued following that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5 in the English, paragraph 2, line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It reads -- and this is something Mr. Traldi asked you about concerning the shelling and the TO and whether it was the reason for the people to depart from the territory. It says as follows: "The TO Staff didn't issue order to open fire on Bosanski Novi territory, except for Blagaj where warning shots were fired when the military police was attacked." Are you familiar with the sequence of events? Was there first the attack on the military police, or first were these warning shells fired first?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, logic dictates that there must have been an incident first involving the military police for the shells to be fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you not tell us what logic is but would you tell us what you know about it. If you have specific information, tell us; if you don't have, then tell us as well. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to preserve a very specific objection: These matters are all addressed in the witness's statement, and we continue not to consider this an efficient use of court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So now I cannot even re-direct on something that was directly crossed, cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that's the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think that it's the position of the Prosecution that it's mainly repetitious in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I would agree with that and say while the document came in -- using parts of the document that weren't asked about to restate evidence in this statement is perhaps not what the Chamber intended to address in its decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, at the same time, Mr. Traldi, this, of course, relates now to how it was described in the document. That is a new element in the -- it's not just the what the witness tells us. But at the same time the witness often, as he showed in his answer to the last question, is talking about logic. We're not interested in -- well, we're interested in logic but not necessarily the witness's logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I correctly noticed, and my question was if this witness has knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and he doesn't have it. He says -- he starts explaining about logic, so apparently he has no knowledge. Otherwise, he would have told us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasic, it is the Judges' impression that you have no knowledge of this. Do you have any personal knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I apologise for having caused confusion. It was not my intention. I received that piece of information. It was reported to me immediately after those events. First, there was the incident involving the attack on the military patrol of the TO Staff and then the warning shells were fired. We used radio communication at the time since the telephone lines were down and I lived outside of the centre of Novi Grad. They got in touch with me, and I came to the town. At around 1.00 in the morning that day, we called Mr. Muhamedagic to try and calm the situation down. He responded to it and was quite co-operative in an attempt to deal with the problem. Together with the TO Staff commander, I was there, as well as Mr. Muhamedagic, SDA president, at the TO Staff. We were trying to come up with a solution in order to put a stop to what was going on. I think I mention it in my statement. Mr. Muhamedagic even issued a written statement and made a statement on Novi Grad radio. It was in the morning at around 4.00 or 5.00 a.m. It was an extraordinary broadcast. Mr. Muhamedagic called upon the Muslim population, those who were armed and who were extremists, to abstain from any opening fire so as to be able to deal with the problem during the day. Once the night was over, we hoped to be able to find a solution during the next day. That is the extent of my knowledge. I partially participated directly in what was going on but only in that part. I participated in those events in terms of specific things. In other words, I was not in the area of Blagaj but I was at the TO Staff command down-town. Blagaj is 6 to 7 kilometres away from Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I take the witness back to one of his previous answers. There was a -- it was read to you that -- that Mr. Traldi had asked about shelling. Now, Mr. Lukic, I think you are talking about warning shells? Could you tell us exactly --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It's page 9, line 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- no, but you are talking about warning shells, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what the document is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you tell us, Witness, exactly whether these warning shells, did they -- did they hit any persons or houses or that they just explode in a meadow without any damage apart from damage to the meadow and perhaps one or two cows? Could you tell us about the warning shells, how many were there? Could you tell us where they landed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yesterday already I said that the then-TO Staff formation had that type of infantry weaponry at its disposal. I think they were 60-millimetre mortars. These warning shells were fired on a meadow, as you said yourself. There was no destruction or human casualties, unless you consider the meadow itself. But they weren't fired at any houses or at people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they also did not hit any houses, did not hit any people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do you know? Do you have any knowledge apart from what others told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the second or third day, it -- I would have found out had they lied to me, but they hadn't. They told me that they did it for psychological effect. They fired those shells on a meadow close to the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say you were told that they never hit any house or no person was affected by it, and you said what you saw a few days later would confirm that information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I didn't see it. Please. When I queried what had happened the day before and even before that, people told me that nothing was damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you verified that because you said on the second or third day, I would have found out if they lied to me but they hadn't. How were you able to establish that they had not lied to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, some things could be subsequently checked, not perhaps at the same time with any reliability, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, tell us, then, what you checked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely that. I spoke to Mr. Muhamedagic. I asked him whether he knew of anyone being hurt or killed or somebody's house being destroyed. He confirmed that, fortunately, it was not the case. So at that point in time there was no destruction, no damage. That was the knowledge I obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you first received information and a few days later you heard from -- I always have difficulties in pronouncing his name, but the SDA representative you received information that, indeed, no house was damaged, no person was hit by any shell, but you didn't observe it personally. You didn't go in the field and you saw that all the houses were intact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's the break time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is. Could you tell us how much more time you would uses -- you would need, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope I'll finish in the next 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we have only two witnesses today and tomorrow, so we'll finish both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We take a break. Witness, you are invited to follow the usher, and we'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasic, we do not have much time and yet we have a number of topics to deal with. I would kindly ask you for precise answer, and if you believe it necessary to explain some things, do go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will need P7103 on our screens again. We were on page 3 in B/C/S and on page 5 in English. So paragraph 2 in English on the page 5, and the second-last paragraph in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to what we have already discussed, we also see here that the TO Staff commander says as follows. It was his estimate that he could not preserve control over the entire municipality and that some groups are distancing themselves from the chain of command, are not obeying orders, and are acting on their own initiative. Such large number of armed people should be placed under control. He adds by saying that certain groups of people are engaging in looting, and various armed groups introducing themselves as regular units, whereas in fact we they operate under no one's control and command and are engaging in looting activities. Next it is stated on the same page, it is the second paragraph from the bottom in the English, that: "The Crisis Staff analysed the situation and distanced itself from the activities carried out by such illegal groups and that this conclusion was reached on the 13th of May." You proposed the following, and I will ask you about how much of it was implemented. It reads -- it is on the next page in the B/C/S. "Simultaneously, all bodies have been instructed" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have lost our English version. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "At the same time, all the bodies have been instructed and fully authorised to undermine the work and activity of the aforementioned illegal individuals, that is, to remove them from the territory of the municipality." During the same session, a binding conclusion was issued to the municipal TO Staff to have its military police units, with the assistance of the police units from the SJB, and if need be with engaging the military police from the Banja Luka Corps, carry out an assessment of the situation and undertake specific measures of mopping up terrain in the parts of town where there had been incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have the last page that was here, please. This is not the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we have to go to page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's on page 5 in English, the lower part of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could it be enlarged by deleting the frame on the right side? Thank you. And the same perhaps in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "They should also introduce public law and order and ensure the possibility for civilians to return to the area." Mr. Pasic, following the 13th of May, were you successful in bringing the tensions down and in disarming these groups, or did the situation become worse?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does refresh my memory. I remember that we asked for the situation to be calmed down but it did not, it wasn't, as can be seen from a number of documents. There were groups beyond anyone's control as specified here. However, we tried our best to introduce normal life and law and order. Unfortunately, the war was already under way, and there were incidents on both sides making the situation worse from one day to the next. It became worse by the day. We really tried to ask those competent bodies, such as the TO Staff and the civilian police, to intervene. The basic problem was the one we've already mentioned. There was a shortage of personnel, operative personnel, and also equipment. We discussed that issue a moment ago when we talked about weapons and equipment for the needs of the military and the police. That was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us briefly look at page 5 in the B/C/S and 7 in the English, the last paragraph in the English, meaning we'll need to go to the next page there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the third paragraph from the bottom, where it says: "On the 20th of May, a session of the Municipal SDS Board was held, where an analysis was taken of the political and security situation in the field -- in the municipality, and three important positions were adopted."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do we have the right page in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to turn it to another page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, it's page 7 that was asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Until now we were on the right page. Now I can continue. We just need the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can we see the bottom of this page. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I just read. And we have to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, three important positions were taken, according to the document. Let's see what they are. "1: All citizens who want to move out voluntarily from the area of Bosanski Novi must be allowed to do so unobstructed." "2: Strictly forbid any measures and activities that would be directed at the -- the forceful moving out of the citizens. "3: All the citizens who decided to reside in the area of the Bosanski Novi municipality must give their unambiguous insurances of total loyalty to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." I need to read out the following paragraph in relation to this and then I'll have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English, it the first full paragraph; and, in the B/C/S, it goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "We saw the conclusions of the SDS but it seems that the Crisis Staff met on May 27th. At its session it acknowledged the stands of the SO SDS on relocation and conclusions from the SDS and SDA representatives' sessions held the previous day, at which stands and political decisions on voluntary location were accepted [Realtime transcript read in error "excepted"]."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "Accepted," which means something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Accepted, yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Not "expected."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They were made an exception of?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. They accepted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh. Well, if you look at the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, you noticed actually the wrong translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, in the original, it says "where the positions were accepted." Mr. Pasic, did you take part in this meeting of the SDS Crisis Staff and the meeting with the representatives of the SDA when this was discussed on these dates, the 20th, the 22nd of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did take part in the Crisis Staff, that's for sure. I think that I was at the SDS meeting too. I'm -- I was a member of the SDS. I belonged to this political orientation, so as part of the leadership. So 90 per cent of the meetings I did attend. As for this other one, I'm not going to claim with 100 per cent certainty that I was there at all meetings with the SDA, but I was there at most of the meetings. So I'm aware of this subject matter as referred to here in this written text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In talks during those days with the representatives of the SDA or anybody else during those days, did they accept, did they -- did they express their views regarding these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can say that this was more and more pronounced by the representatives of the SDA and these people who represented the Muslim people; namely, that they wanted to leave the area. I mentioned that in my statement too, what the reasons were, what the motives were for them to leave the area of the municipality of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me briefly remind you of something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 9, paragraph 2 in the English; and page 6, paragraph 2, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
