utterances.text: You see the second paragraph here underneath the long one? It says: "The population in Blagaj remained without a solution so one was sought for its migration. Negotiations were held with the organs of the Autonomous Region with the government of the Serbian Republic of Krajina and UNPROFOR. The remaining possibility was to expedite a voluntary emigration towards Banja Luka and that a return to the valley of Japra was definitely impossible, but this population showed no willingness for that." Did you take part in the negotiations when this proposal was refused by the population of the Japra river valley, when they refused to move in the direction of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that time-period, attempts were made in respect of the territories that were under Serb control, if I can put it that way, that this part of the population should be moved to that area in depth because we thought they'd be safer there. It would go on for a day or two. We thought that by then the situation would have been normalised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was did you take part in the negotiations. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I've been trying to say. I am aware of this fact and I am saying what the intention was of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but that wasn't the question. The question was not what intentions there were. The question was whether you participated in those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware of that. I think I did take part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you take part or not? Think? I mean, we're not interested in your thoughts. We're interested in what your recollection is as to whether you took part or not. If you know, tell us; if you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is hard to give that kind of answer, simply because there were many questions that interacted in that period. I think that I am a participant in this situation, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, next question, please. The witness apparently is not inclined to give a direct answer to the question. Next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who conveyed the proposals to the population of Blagaj, these proposals to move? How did this function? Tell us briefly. Who tells their representatives, who are these representatives, who conveys this to the population?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had their own representatives from their own ethnic community and they attended these meetings when conclusions would be agreed upon. So they were supposed to move to the interior, and the representatives of the Muslim population were there and they conveyed it to them. So it's not that we directly went out into the field and that we talked to the masses. Rather, we spoke to the representatives of these people, and then they were the intermediaries, they were the ones who conveyed this further, who explained to these people what the proposals were, what the proposals and conclusions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. In view of these answers, could you tell us -- we're talking about thousands of people, if I understand well. Was it verified that everyone who was leaving agreed with that, or was it just that you accepted that they all wanted to leave without verifying whether that would be true for all individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was impossible to go from house to house and from individual to individual. We worked with their representatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again, I'm not asking what was possible. I asked whether it was verified, and I do understand your answer to be that it was not verified on an individual basis. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood that correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us how many remained in the area, where most of people left or all of them left? Could you tell us how many households still would remain -- remained in the area at the time? I mean Bosnian households.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately then. Was it ten, was it 100, was it 500? Households; I'm talking about households.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, households, it's very hard to say. Perhaps it's easier to speak of the number of inhabitants. I think about 500 so or remained, but how many I really wouldn't dare say. I don't think it would be an accurate answer if I were to give you any particular figure now. I think it was somewhat over 500 but that is not a reliable or accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they originate from specific villages or was it from all villages, a very small number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think it was from several villages, not just one village. Several.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And why do you think that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think, in view of the situation that later -- I mean, over a period of time, that is to say, during the war some people appeared who were not only from Blagaj but Suhaca, Agici, some of these typically Muslim villages. How many of them were there, it's hard to say. I mean, later, in that period, you couldn't know where they came from or how many were there, but in view of the sequence of events that followed in 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995 we would learn, say, that there is somebody there from Gornji Agici who is living there, who stayed on ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us a few examples which -- do you remember Mr. X, Mr. Y who stayed and in what village he stayed, or, if it's a she, where she stayed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, really. I mean, I don't know because I was not prepared for that. Perhaps that could have been the case if some checks were to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at this moment I'm asking what your recollection is. Could you tell us whether there's still -- those who stayed, are they still living in the same municipality, to the extent you know. If you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean nowadays whether they're living there now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Or whether you know what happened to them in the last, well, let's say, 20 years? Whether they stayed after the war, whether they -- do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly part of that Muslim population stayed on during the war then and after the war, too. And I think they're still living there. Now, I mean, biologically, whether somebody died a natural death, that I don't know. But I know that there are some people there and that there are people who had left the area and who returned and who are living there right now although they left during the war. You can see that on the basis of renovated houses in these villages that these people returned, and now they live a most normal live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many did return, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have an exact figure. Right now, I'm not in the municipal organs. But there are some figures to the effect that part of the population had returned and that part of the population is coming from time to time, coming on vacation, they work in other countries, and then they spend their vacations there, and then they live there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're getting close to the end, Mr. Pasic. It's not going to take very long. We've come to the stadium now. My colleague Mr. Traldi asked you on page -- LiveNote page 10, line 7. You spoke about this train that went to Doboj, women, children, the elderly continue their journey; able-bodied men return, are put up at the Mlakve stadium. At this stadium, Mlakve, was anybody killed there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of. As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the stadium, did these people go away. They did leave at some point, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, all these reception centres as we called them at that time, so one of them was the Mlakve stadium. I mean, all these people on that last day when the refugees left they all went in the direction of Croatia and to third countries out into the world. Nobody stayed on after that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, thank you. That's all that we had for you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, do you have any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just about five minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Further cross-examination by Mr. Traldi:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we could stick with this same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And have the bottom of page 7 in the English and what I believe is the bottom of page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While that comes up you were asked about shelling, and in that context, you said you heard that there was no destruction or human casualties when warning shells were fired at Blagaj on or around 12th of May, 1992, but you didn't go to the area. You do know that after the mortars fired at Muslim villages in the Japra valley later that month and the disarming operations, many men were killed in the Japra valley, many houses and other structures were set on fire, and those villages were completely looted? You know those things to be true; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, let's have, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, I'm looking for the bottom of page 8 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this follows immediately on the paragraph about the armed activities including the use of mortars that caused the expulsion of Muslim civilians from the victims of G. Agic, Celopek, Hozic, and Suhaca. The next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's the second-to-last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And after that it mentions an order by the Crisis Staff. Below that in the final paragraph the very bottom of the page, we read: "The order was not followed through which led to complete chaos, the villages mentioned were completely looted, and enormous problems appeared in relation to ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then we turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "... Civilian defence. There were men killed, many houses were set on fire, as well as other structures." So in fact you and the rest of the Crisis Staff did know to be true that property in the Japra valley had been looted, that men had been killed there, and that various structures had been set on fire. That's the truth; right.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic asked you if you knew how the Muslims from the Japra valley got to Blagaj. You said: "They believed that a smaller area would be safer for them." They believed it would be safer because of exactly these events that we read about in your Crisis Staff's report; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You won't let me talk. I keep giving short answers, and of course that is confusing. I cannot give answers the way you are putting questions, because this is a very big question and it is too big for just a short answer, and that is probably why I'm going to confuse you, you're not going to get the right picture, you're not going to get to the truth of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, as long as your answers directly relate to what you're asked, then no one stops you. It's only when you start answering all kind of questions that were not put to you, that's where you're stopped. So could you please, instead of criticising the question, could you answer the question. A portion was read to you. The question was: "They believed it would be safer because of exactly these events that we read about in your Crisis Staff's reports..." That that is why they believed that a smaller area would be safer for them. The question was whether you agree with that or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite simply I don't understand such a lengthy question. And what time-period is involved? Is it the beginning of May, mid-May, the end of May, the beginning of June, is it July? I don't know what you're saying. I don't understand you. I'm not criticizing the question. I'm saying that I don't have an answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you did criticise the question, as a matter of fact, and you did criticise us for not allowing you to answer. I think what Mr. Traldi referred to is when the population concentrated in Blagaj. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is in the context of the questions clear to the Chamber, but now it's maybe clear to you as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if we're talking about this period towards the end of May, then this culmination took place, this chaos culminated, if I can put it that way. The situation was indeed very difficult, and the situation was such that certain paramilitary formations caused great problems for us. And of course, at that time there were certain clashes, but there was fire coming were both sides; that is to say, that it wasn't that people were just standing on one side and shooting from the other side. So there was sporadic gun-fire, there was fighting, there were attempts made in certain parts of villages to find out where the shooting was coming from. So all of these are moments that cannot be described in just in two or three words. It is impossible to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might briefly follow up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you just to confirm whether certain proposition that appear in this report are literally true, yes or no. Is it true, yes or no, that the villages in the Japra valley were completed looted as your Crisis Staff wrote in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is from the report and if the Crisis Staff wrote that, I am not opposed to such statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that men were killed in those villages as your Crisis Staff wrote in the report in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where that's written. Can you show me that? Can I see what this is all about? I mean, you are confusing me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, it was read to you when it was read to you that property in the Japra valley had been looted, men had been killed there, and various structures had been set on fire. That is what is in the report. And it was read to you several times, but that is what Mr. Traldi is asking about, whether it's true that men were killed as reported.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look, if men were killed, if the interpretation is right, the question is obviously who was it that left on the 23rd of July, who left then; that's to say, not everybody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we're not talking on a hypothetical basis. The question is whether you can confirm that men in those villages were killed as is stated in that Crisis Staff report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot confirm that given the time distance involved. I really cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. Next question, please, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, how is it that you can recall there was fire coming from different directions, you can recall details that are -- or that suggest there was combat, but you captain recall the information that your Crisis Staff reported in 1992 that reflects the crimes committed against Muslim civilians in that area?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would object to this type of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. Reason for objection is?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you -- how is it that you can recall one thing and you cannot recall another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, sometimes there is an explanation for that and Mr. Traldi explores whether the witness can provide such an information. And if he cannot, he will tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But -- and I would really suggest that Mr. Traldi reads what he wants this gentleman to confirm. It's -- I read that he would remember or maybe he would -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness testified in quite some detail about the events at the time, and the witness also told us that due to the passage of time he doesn't remember whether people were killed as was stated in that report. Mr. Traldi explores with the witness whether he has any explanation why on one matter he still knows the details, while on another matter you does not. And that is the question that the witness is now invited to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, but if you -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic. This is not a detail. This is a ruling, and the witness is invited to answer the question. Do you have any explanation, Mr. Pasic, as why you do remember some details and whereas on this matter your recollection doesn't serve you anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An explanation as to why I remember certain details and others I don't is probably the one that has to do with nature. It's normal. Some things I remember, others I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question please, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Then I have one. I would like to address the parties. There was this huge discussion about whether there was an order to the TO, yes or no, which also appears in this document. A date is mentioned for that order. But as far as I remember, we have not seen that order, and I wonder whether, because there was such a discussion about whether it was an order, a request, and who was competent to give orders, whether there is any written version of that document available -- or of that order, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We'll certainly check, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll check as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll check as well. Okay. Then the Chamber is looking forward to see that. Perhaps the witness could tell us. Do you remember what was so thoroughly discussed whether that order was -- the order of 25th of May, 1992, where this report says: "... issued the order to the TO municipal staff that they should immediately place under its control all its members and units." Do you know whether that was a written order or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I knew who issued the order, I could probably be in a position to give a more specific answer. Otherwise, I can't provide you with an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you carefully listened to what I said and my reference to the discussion, it was the Crisis Staff. As the report reads: "The Crisis Staff reacted briskly and issued the order to the TO municipal staff," and, again, gives a date, 25th of May. Do you know whether that was a written order or whether it was not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. But if there was something, then for the most part it was in written form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I asked you whether you remembered. Not if there was something. The report says that there was an order. I leave it to that. Mr. Pasic, I'd like to thank you very much at this moment where we have concluded to hear your evidence. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered the many questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, and put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again, and you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you and good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what would be -- or Mr. Stojanovic, what we could do is to take the break early again and then we would have -- we would resume at 20 past 1.00 and then have another 55 minutes today. I see Mr. Mladic is nodding yes. So then -- then we'll take the break first, and we'll have the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Defence will then call its next witness. No protective measures. And it would be Mr. Ubiparip. Is that -- yes. We take a break and resume at -- Yes, Mr. Traldi -- oh, you're just standing for the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we resume at 20 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this morning, when the previous witness was about to arrive in the courtroom, you gave the impression that you'd like to respond in some way to what I said about the length of the stay of witnesses here in The Hague. If you'd still want to do that, and if you can do it in a relatively short time, I would give you an opportunity now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I checked with -- actually we checked with the Victims and Witness Unit and actually said that they criticised all three parties. Perhaps you should ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't criticise anyone at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, yes, we brought the first week, that was five-day week, we brought maybe a bit more witnesses. We were cautious maybe we won't have witnesses, and the last week was actually the consequence of that one. But for this week, we envisage that we will finish all the witnesses we called for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The only reason why I specifically addressed the Defence is because you are determining the time when they have to arrive, et cetera, but, of course, it's, I would say, a shared responsibility for all parties to take care that witnesses should not stay too long but since at this moment the Prosecution is not determining when witnesses should arrive but certainly have an effect on how long the examination takes. Therefore, if I gave the impression that I was blaming the Defence for it, I think I asked for closer attention to be given to the matter, and that is exactly what I'm seeking, just to avoid --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can tell you how we organise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We calculate direct and cross and add some time. Sometime we do not add enough time, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. As long as it has your specific attention, the Chamber also noted that the Prosecution is indicating at an early stage whether or not they would cross-examine the witness, and therefore it's -- we consider it to be a shared responsibility. Also responsibility of the Chamber to seek to avoid that witnesses have to stay for a minute longer than necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If I could address one very brief follow-up matter in private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but before the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the witness could remain standby behind the door, but we'll briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I don't know whether someone is waiting behind the doors. If so, then perhaps they could be given a signal that we're ready to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ubiparip, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I would also like to greet everyone present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Ubiparip. Mr. Ubiparip, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find Mr. Stojanovic to your left, standing, and Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Ubiparip.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to apologise for keeping you waiting so long. According to our standard procedure, kindly tell us your first and last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: My name is Vojin Ubiparip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ubiparip, did you at some point give a statement in written form to the Defence of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we have document 65 ter 1D01755 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ubiparip, hopefully in front of you, you will have the possibility to see your statement. My question is: Do you recognise your signature on the first page of the document?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: I do, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to the last page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ubiparip, tell us, please, whether on this page of your statement you recognise your signature and was the date written in your own handwriting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now focus on paragraph 3 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ubiparip, during proofing for your testimony today, did you tell me that you wanted to add something to item 1 in the very first sentence of your statement? In other words, following the full stop, a number of words should be added: "I physically took over my duties on the 25th of August, 1992."

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, first you said we should focus on paragraph 3, and then you said to add something to item 1. I take it that you are referring to paragraph 3 of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, sentence 1. I apologise, Your Honours, if I used the wrong term. So the first sentence of the third paragraph. I correct myself for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ubiparip, being in this courtroom today, having solemnly declared that you will speak the truth, with this addition to your statement, if the same questions were to be put to you, would you provide the same answers and would they reflect the truth and would they be to the best of your recollection, in terms of accuracy?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to tender the statement of Witness Vojin Ubiparip, 65 ter number 1D01755.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01755 receives Exhibit D891, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D891 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, I'd like to read out Mr. Ubiparip's summary. Witness Vojin Ubiparip is a professional military officer. He is a colonel. When the war broke out in BiH, he was in Serbia on his tour of duty. Given the fact that he hails from BiH, having been invited to do so, he reported to the Main Staff of the VRS on the 19th of August, 1992. As of the 25th of August, 1992, he took over the duty of commander of the 1st Battalion of the 22nd Light Infantry Brigade of the 1st Krajina Corps in the sector of Vlasic. Between late January and June 1993, he held the position of Chief of Staff of that brigade. As of June 1993 until the end of the war, he was the commander of the Kotor Varos Brigade of the VRS. In his testimony, the witness will discuss the relationship between the VRS and his unit and paramilitary formations, as well as to resistance lent against the intention to politicise the army, as well as the fact that his unit also included officers who were of Muslim or Croat ethnicity. He will point out his good relationship and co-operation with his colleague, officer of Bosniak ethnicity, who at the time was the security organ of the 1st Krajina Corps Command. He will further testify that he was in contact with persons of Muslim ethnicity who told him that the leadership of the SDA ordered them to leave Kotor Varos. If they failed to do so, they would be killed. That way, the SDA leadership, making use of fear and panic, exercised pressure on the Muslims to leave the area of Kotor Varos. There were prisoners of war taken by his unit in the operations it participated. They were treated in keeping with the laws and customs of war. The prisoners of war were, for a while, located in the village of Siprage, and a list of the POWs was handed over to the Red Cross as well. In terms of an incident in the village of Vrbanjci, this witness has only indirect knowledge about the events there. When General Mladic visited his unit, he constantly pointed out that it was necessary that the army respected the laws, customs, and rules of war, and the Geneva Conventions. This, Your Honour, concludes the summary of this witness's statement, and I have only a few questions in order to clarify a couple of points from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put your questions to the witness, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please have D891, paragraph 7, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is your statement, Mr. Ubiparip. In paragraph 7, you say that, under your command, you had subordinate officers who were Muslims and Croats. Given our courtroom practice, try to be specific and tell the Chamber, to the best of your recollection, if you can, how many such commissioned officers and non-commissioned officers were there, and, if possible, their first and last names?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: It was a long time but I remember it well. There was Major Asim Adembegovic, who was my assistant commander for logistics for a while. From the then TO Staff in Kotor Varos, there was an NCO of Croat ethnicity, I've forgot his name. Later on, that person was in the technical department of my unit. On top of that, in terms of lending assistance, we sporadically engaged somebody whose name eludes me for the moment, but later on this person became the minister of justice in Republika Srpska as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at paragraph 23 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, the situation you described was the situation in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mentioned two officers or non-commissioned officers, out of how many officers in the brigade all together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember two. One of them was a friend of mine, the logistics man, and this other one, well, you know. Mr. President, there has been so many of them. So many names. I've simply forgotten. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you two out of a total of how many officers and commissioned officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the brigade? Well, in the brigade command, there were over 20 that were linked to the staff, logistics, and operative work. Operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in the brigade as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that 1st Brigade, it was at first such that it had the form of a company, but eventually it turned into a strong brigade. Towards the end of the war, it reorganised and got stronger.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to hear how many officers and non-commissioned officers there were in the brigade at that time. Not how it developed over time but how it was in June 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 15 to 20, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you said only in the brigade command there were 20 already, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The total. The total. In the brigade command, up until 8 or 10, when I took over the brigade. As for the other officers, they were company commanders and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at paragraph 23 in document D891.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ubiparip, you have before you that document. You can follow it. You spoke about this fact that you had meetings with General Mladic, and I would like to ask you, yet again, to try to spell this out in more concrete terms. To the best of your recollection, how many times did you meet with General Mladic during the war, and if you can tell us where this happened?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: This is the way it was. I first met General Mladic on the 19th of August at Han Pijesak, that's where the command of the Main Staff was, and he briefly informed us there and said to us that all of us who came from particular places should take our units to our places of birth. And then after the regrouping, I was transferred by bus to Bijeljina where I spent the night, and in the morning hours of the 20th we set out towards Banja Luka, towards the corps command there. The second time, I saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go to the second time you saw him, you met him the first time on the 19th of August of which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, that's right. August, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second time I saw the general was in the month of May 1993. I was Chief of Staff then of the 22nd Brigade and Operations Group Vlasic as well. Our commander briefed us about the current situation in the Army of Republika Srpska, the security situation, et cetera. However, what mattered for me was that an aide-memoire was being elaborated for all members of the VRS. And this included an annex that had to do with the Geneva Convention and the Helsinki Agreements as well. I can tell you one thing: When we got that in our unit that I commanded, nothing happened that would in a certain way have the status of something that would be irregular, let alone a crime. Anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next opportunity to meet General Mladic, the next meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: The next one was in 1994, September, October, in Doboj, where there was this meeting that involved an analysis at the level of the Main Staff and all commanders of brigades. The last time I saw the general was around the 5th of May, 1995. I remember that well. In Mrkonjic Grad. A meeting was organised there that had to do with raising combat readiness and taking measures in terms of strengthening in order to prevent erosion. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ubiparip. I'm just going to put one more question to you in order to make things more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at paragraph 20 of your statement, D891.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you can see this, you said that you had POWs from these operations that you took part in?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be more precise and could you tell the Trial Chamber to the best of your recollection where were these POWs, was that the result of combat, and what was the number involved?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was: Combat took place in the form of defence in the southeastern part of Vlasic in the Travnik area and where the Biljana and Vrbanja rivers are, at Ljuta Greda, Recica, Jasen, Svinjska Glava, that's where we organised defence and since already by then the 7th Corps of the BiH Army had been established with the basic task of carrying out a breakthrough. My brigade was the weakest link in that chain, and it was supposed to take the axis of Travnik-Kotor Varos-Derventa and Bosanski Brod, and then in that way Republika Srpska would be cut in two parts. And then at the second stage - since these were mostly people who were the so-called expellees from Bosanska Krajina, you see - that would follow. However, this objective was not obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But the question was --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: In this combat there were these prisoners. I remember that I first took three of them prisoner, and I had contact with the corps commander and until then there weren't any POWs. And I told Mehmedalagic, since he used to my superior officer, I said, "Let us stick to the convention, the Geneva Convention on warfare," and I was the first one to give them first aid and food, these POWs, I reported them to the Red Cross and so on. And I can tell you one thing: That on the other side also there was no abuse as far as our soldiers were concerned who were taken prisoner. So there was general progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your exhaustive answers, Mr. Witness, and at this moment we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. MacDonald, are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ubiparip, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. MacDonald. You find him to your right. And Mr. MacDonald is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ubiparip.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You spoke with my friend Mr. Stojanovic and the Presiding Judge about the number of officers in the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade when you became commander in June 1993. The commander previous to you was Dusan Novakovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have P00851 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Ubiparip, this is a list of officers in the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade, and it has been dated to sometime between the end of August and December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I believe we only need the B/C/S for my question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then ... yes, it's now on our screen. And?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Ubiparip, there are 21 names on this page.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ubiparip, there are another 21 names on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And if we could move to the final page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And there are 15 names on this page. Now, by my calculation, that makes 57 officers at the end of 1992. Are you sure when you took over in June of 1993 that there were only 20 officers in your unit?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Well, when I personally toured the units, the ones that I took over, from Chief of Staff down to company commanders, that's the number that I got to. However, since everything was following apart, and everything was falling apart, and later on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: And speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to come closer to the microphone and speak into it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I assumed my duty of commander of the Kotor Varos Brigade, when I toured the units and when I took over, on the spot, I identified about 20 of them. It is possible that beforehand they had been built into the establishment, but I don't know where it was that they had been. It is only later that I made additional efforts to reorganise and we created a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Do I understand by your answer, sir, that you accept when you took over there could have been more officers but as commander you were simply unaware of them?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I didn't know, I didn't know. I mean, later on, when I really -- I mean, at first, I was supposed to take care of combat operations. And later on when I had time, I looked at our files, our documents, and then I -- Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the simple "yes" you have answered the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: One final question on this document, Mr. Ubiparip. Out of the 57 names under the word "nationality" in the second-last column, they are all recorded as Serbian apart from two, and the two that are not recorded are on the page in front of us. You'll see an Azem Aganbegovic [phoen] recorded as Yugoslavia and another name --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: -- without nationality recorded. Do you accept that of the 57 officers only two were non-Serbian?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd like to move onto a new topic. You say in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And we can finish with this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You say in your statement at paragraph 7 you were appointed commander of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade in June of 1993. What date exactly did you take that position?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: On the 10th of June, I received information. I was on leave, and according to plan, I was to return as Chief of Staff of the 22nd Brigade in Vlasic. My driver met me and he ordered me to proceed towards Kotor Varos, because according to the order of the corps commander I was urgently reassigned -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're giving us the whole story, whereas only the date was asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we need further details, then we'll ask you for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 10th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The Defence has led evidence that the command post of the 1st Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade was moved from Kotor Varos to the village of Siprage in the second half of 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: That is right. And that took place at my initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: When exactly in the second half of 1993 did it move?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Well, in view of the distance from the front line, it was illogical for the command to be that far away. So I started moving it and gradually it came to the front line at Jasen. Do you understand what I'm saying? Officially it was in Siprage; however, the command was non-stop on the very first positions, and that's where the strength of the unit was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: When was it officially in Siprage?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: From October, roughly, 1993. It was in Siprage. Do you understand that? And until the end of the war, it was officially in ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Could you just repeat the very end of your sentence. Until the end of the war, it was officially in?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: In Siprage. The brigade command, the command of the Kotor Varos Brigade. Do you understand what I'm saying? Until the end of the war, it was in Siprage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The Defence has also led evidence that the logistics of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade was based in Siprage village. No specific date is given for that, although surrounding events are placed in 1992. Do you know exactly when the logistics of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade was first based in Siprage village?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: I'll explain you the stages --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can I stop you there, please, sir. Just one moment. Can you just tell us if you know when it was first based there; and, if you do know, tell us the date. That is all.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Say, in late August or in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Is that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'll move on. The 2nd Battalion of the 22nd Brigade moved out of the Kotor Varos municipality by the end of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: After that, was the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade the only VRS military unit on the territory of the Kotor Varos municipality until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss the village of Siprage in more detail now. Siprage village swore loyalty to Republika Srpska and surrendered weapons at the outbreak of the conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes, that was before my arrival. They were all in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 11 of your statement, you say you were informed that the mosque in the village of Siprage was destroyed. That destruction took place around the end of June 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Hmm ... July or August? Something like that. In that period in any case. I have to tell you straight away that I was against the destruction of religious buildings. I undertook all measures to prevent that because it was an ugly site --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can I stop you there again please, sir. Thank you for answering my question. July or August, is that in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Are you aware that other mosques had been destroyed in Kotor Varos municipality since the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: When I first came in Kotor Varos to assume my duty on the 10th of June, I was really disappointed by what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, sir, were you aware that other mosques had been destroyed previous to the mosque in Siprage since the outbreak of the conflict in Kotor Varos municipality?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Well, the only mosque that was not destroyed at the time was the one in Siprage. All of the others were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Turning to the mosque in Siprage. In paragraph 11 of your statement, you say that Mujko Zuhric told you that the paramilitaries had done this?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You didn't conduct any investigation into the destruction of the mosque in Siprage then; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: This is how it was: I went on leave as planned, and when I returned, Mujko told me that the mosque had been destroyed by paramilitaries and that the civilian police in Kotor Varos was investigating it. I had no authority to launch a separate investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And just for the record, you did not launch any kind of investigation, did you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: I didn't. Because it was within the competence of the civilian police and the local authorities in the municipality where my unit was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: So your knowledge about what happened to Siprage mosque comes from what Mujko Zuhric told you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd seek to call up a document now. I'd ask out of an abundance of caution that it not be broadcast. Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 31881. And I'm looking for page 2 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Ubiparip, this is a statement of a Muslim from Kotor Varos municipality dealing with events in Siprage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm looking for the paragraph beginning: "On 25th June 1993 ..." In the B/C/S it is at the top --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, we have it in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It reads: "On 25 June 1993, the mosque in Siprage was destroyed by the Chetniks from Vlasic, commanded by Stanko Trivic." My question, Mr. Ubiparip: There was no officer called Stanko Trivic based in Vlasic in June 1993, was there?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: No. There was Janko Trivic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. And on 25th June 1993, Janko Trivic was the commander of the 22nd Brigade. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And the 22nd Brigade at this time was based in Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Did you ever hear at the time of these events, allegations that forces commanded by Trivic had destroyed the mosque in Siprage?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I apologise. This question may be confusing. Which Trivic? Because two were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it was also established that there was only one, which was by the name of Janko. Apart from that, the question has been answered. The objection would have been denied. Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If I can take you back to the statement, Mr. Ubiparip, I'm just going to read on. The author states: "After that, we asked to move out and they promised us that we would move our...," I believe that is meant to be the word "out," "... but that we first had to hand over our white goods, cattle, and cars." Did you hear about this, Mr. Ubiparip?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have the exhibit back on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It was 31881. That is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Page 2 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Do you recall the question, Mr. Ubiparip?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP
utterances.text: I do. As far as I knew, never was it even considered that they would hand over their vehicles and household items, nor was it at all within my competence as brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm going to ask for another document, Your Honours. Again, if it may not be broadcast for the same reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do, I just want to ask a question. But do you remember this incident that these people had to leave, had to move out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you part of the operation that asked them to move out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't there personally but some of the leading men came to see me, given the fact that I had helped them before with providing food and securing transport, they told me to complain that they were instructed from the headquarters. What they said was that they had to move towards Central Bosnia and Sarajevo, and if they failed to do that, they were threatened with their closest ones being destroyed. It was awful for me to hear that and I felt very sorry for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Headquarters of what? What headquarters were these that ordered them to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My communications officer was this Mujko Zuhric who was also in the corps command. He was a Bosniak. He gave me information about the things going on and who was collecting information and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you. My question was what headquarters was this that ordered that they leave? Is it the headquarters of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know personally, but they said "centrala," the centre or the headquarters, be it political or military. I have no clue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And who are these leaders who are telling you this? You said leaders came to tell you that the headquarters said they must leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The more prominent people came to see me as a delegation, and Mujko was there as well. They expressed their regrets for having to leave because they were threatened by their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their people in Siprage. According to my knowledge, the people didn't want to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask on one point of clarification. You said you don't know whether they received instructions from the civilian or the military headquarters. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how your words are transcribed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said. I don't know what structures were involved, military or civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time in your statement at paragraph 12 we read that it was the SDA which, as far as I understand, is a civilian structure. Do you have any explanation as to why you refer there to the SDA leadership and tell us now that you don't whether it was military or civilian authority that instructed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, when I was battalion commander up there at the Vlasic plateau, I was in charge of securing the corridor for the exchange of populations. All those from western Bosnia moving via Vlasic, I asked them and they mostly said that they were ordered by "centrala" in Sarajevo that they had to move out. I asked them whether there were no longer able to live where they lived before, and they all said no, that they had to listen to their "centrala" to go there. That is why I believe there was some SDA involvement in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you believe, but that's your conclusion on the basis of the word "centrala"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Well, we are at a point where we have to adjourn. Mr. Ubiparip, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.30, in this same courtroom. But before you leave this courtroom, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that's clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you earlier said we would have two witnesses. That means that the witness after this one is on standby for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, the witness after this one is on standby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because I do understand that the time estimate was one hour of cross-examination, Mr. MacDonald, and you'll stick to that. Then we will adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 5th of February, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 5th day of February, 2015, at 9.30 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
